content: This document provides a detailed overview of particles in particle physics, including both currently known and hypothetical elementary particles, as well as composite particles that can be formed from them. Elementary Particles Elementary particles are fundamental entities with no measurable internal structure, meaning they are not composed of smaller particles. These particles are the foundational components of quantum field theory. They are categorized based on their intrinsic angular momentum, or spin. Particles with half-integer spin are called fermions, while those with integer spin are referred to as bosons. The Standard Model The Standard Model of particle physics represents the current theoretical framework for understanding elementary particles and their interactions. All particles predicted by the Standard Model, except the Higgs boson, have been experimentally observed. Fermions (Half-Integer Spin) Fermions possess a spin of ½ and are the fundamental building blocks of matter. Each fermion has a corresponding antiparticle. Fermions are further classified based on their interaction with the color force (a fundamental force mediated by gluons). The Standard Model identifies 12 types of elementary fermions: six quarks and six leptons. Quarks: Quarks interact via the color force and exist in six flavors: up, down, strange, charm, bottom, and top. Their antiparticles are called antiquarks. Leptons: Leptons do not interact via the color force. Their antiparticles are called antileptons. For example, the antiparticle of the electron is the positron. The six leptons are: Electron and positron Electron neutrino and electron antineutrino Muon and antimuon Muon neutrino and muon antineutrino Tau lepton and antitauon Tau neutrino and tau antineutrino Bosons (Integer Spin) Bosons have whole-number spins and mediate the fundamental forces of nature. Gauge bosons are responsible for these forces, while the Higgs boson is hypothesized to generate mass. According to the Standard Model, the elementary bosons include: The Higgs boson (spin-0), which is essential for explaining the origin of particle masses through the Higgs mechanism. This process involves spontaneous symmetry breaking of the SU(2) gauge symmetry. While the Higgs boson is a critical component of the Standard Model, it had not been observed until the Large Hadron Collider experiments at CERN. Hypothetical Particles Several theoretical models, such as supersymmetry, predict the existence of additional particles, though none have been experimentally confirmed as of 2008. Examples include: Photino (spin-½): The supersymmetric partner of the photon. Gluino (spin-½): The supersymmetric partner of the gluon. Gravitino (spin-3/2): The supersymmetric partner of the graviton in supergravity theories. Neutralino (spin-½): A superposition of the supersymmetric partners of neutral Standard Model particles. The lightest neutralino is a leading candidate for dark matter. Charginos: Supersymmetric partners of charged bosons. Sterile Neutrinos: Hypothetical particles introduced in extensions of the Standard Model to explain certain experimental anomalies, such as the LSND results. Sleptons and Squarks (spin-0): Supersymmetric partners of Standard Model fermions. The stop squark (partner of the top quark) is theorized to have a low mass and is a focus of experimental searches. Other theories propose additional bosons, such as: Graviton (spin-2): A particle hypothesized to mediate gravity in quantum gravity theories. Axion (spin-0): A pseudoscalar particle introduced in Peccei-Quinn theory to resolve the strong CP problem. Branon: Predicted in brane-world models. Magnetic Monopole: A particle with non-zero magnetic charge, predicted by some grand unified theories (GUTs). Tachyon: A hypothetical particle that travels faster than the speed of light and has an imaginary rest mass. Composite Particles Composite particles are formed from combinations of elementary particles. They include: Hadrons Hadrons are strongly interacting composite particles, classified as: Baryons: Composite fermions made of three valence quarks (e.g., protons and neutrons). Protons consist of two up quarks and one down quark (uud). Neutrons consist of two down quarks and one up quark (ddu). Hyperons, such as Λ, Σ, Ξ, and Ω particles, contain one or more strange quarks and are heavier and short-lived compared to nucleons. Mesons: Composite bosons made of a valence quark and a valence antiquark (e.g., pions, kaons, and J/ψ particles). Mesons mediate the strong force between nucleons in quantum hadrodynamic models. Exotic hadrons, such as tetraquarks (two quarks and two antiquarks) and glueballs (bound states of gluons), may also exist, though their existence remains uncertain. Atomic Nuclei Atomic nuclei are composed of protons and neutrons. Each nucleus is defined by its specific number of protons and neutrons, referred to as a nuclide or isotope. Nuclear reactions can transform one nuclide into another. Atoms Atoms are the smallest neutral particles that retain the chemical properties of an element. They consist of a dense nucleus surrounded by a cloud of electrons. Each type of atom corresponds to a specific chemical element. To date, 117 elements have been discovered, with atomic numbers ranging from 1 to 118. Molecules Molecules are the smallest units of a substance that retain its physical properties. They are composed of one or more atoms bonded together. Each type of molecule corresponds to a specific chemical compound. Condensed Matter The equations governing condensed matter physics share similarities with those of high-energy particle physics. This allows the application of particle physics theories to condensed matter systems. Quasiparticles, which are field excitations, can be studied in this context. Examples include: Phonons: Vibrational modes in a crystal lattice. Excitons: Bound states of an electron and a hole. Plasmons: Coherent excitations of a plasma. Polaritons: Mixtures of photons with other quasiparticles. Polarons: Moving charged particles surrounded by ions in a material. Magnons: Coherent excitations of electron spins in a material. Other Notable Particles WIMPs (Weakly Interacting Massive Particles): Hypothetical particles that may explain dark matter, such as neutralinos or axions. Goldstone Bosons: Massless excitations resulting from spontaneous symmetry breaking. Instantons: Field configurations representing local minima of the Euclidean action, used in non-perturbative calculations. Dyons: Hypothetical particles with both electric and magnetic charges. Inflaton: A scalar particle responsible for cosmic inflation. Classification by Speed Particles can also be classified based on their speed: Tardyons (Bradyons): Particles that travel slower than the speed of light and have non-zero rest mass. Luxons: Particles that travel at the speed of light and have no rest mass. Tachyons: Hypothetical particles that travel faster than the speed of light and have imaginary rest mass.
